Results — 05/15/26

Exclusions

  • Excluded participants who did not get >= 60% of test trials (one option dominates the other) in the last two-thirds of the task (same criteria as Gail).
  • 49 participants were excluded, leaving 125 participants.
  • Slightly more child participants were excluded.

Learning Phase results

Participants learn well, regardless of age

  • Only includes trials in which one machine’s expected value is greater than the other. Error bars are 95% CI.
  • After exclusions, performance across age groups was very similar.

Participants show a negativity bias overall

knitr::include_graphics("learning_plots/age_valence_asymm.png")

  • Unlike Gail and Noam, we do not see a stronger negativity bias in older participants.
  • No age-related differences in model-derived valence asymmetry in learning rate.

Memory Phase results

Memory performance isn’t great

knitr::include_graphics("memory_plots/age_groups_average_heatmap_facet.png")

  • Performance isn’t amazing.
  • Children seem to be doing better than adults.

Let’s first consider old trials…

The following regression was run

response (old, similar, new) ~ PE sign * PE magnitude * Valence Bias * Age + (1 + PE sign * PE magnitude | ID) Here we treat old as the reference response category because it is the accurate response for these trials. Here’s a table with the results of the regression (source: old_mblogit_summary.txt). In the tables below, green shading marks p < .05 and yellow marks .05 ≤ p < .10.

This is a lot. So let’s plot this to help us make sense of what’s going on.

How does PE magnitude, PE sign, and valence bias shape whether someone will recognize an “old” item?

knitr::include_graphics("memory_plots/valence_asymm_pe_sign_magnitude_old_trials.png")

  • The larger the PE, the more likely the associated item was to be remembered (pe sign, new: p<.001).
  • Individuals with a positivity bias were less likely to mistake an old item as similar (valence asymm, similar: p=.036).
  • For individuals with a negativity bias, positive PEs were more likely to be forgotten and deemed “new” (pe sign, new: p=.04). But those with a positivity bias did not sho w have a difference in performance between positive and negative PEs (pe sign x valence asymm, new: <.001; similar: p=.05)
  • No interaction between PE sign and magnitude.

Do these effects differ with age?

knitr::include_graphics("memory_plots/age_valence_asymm_pe_sign_magnitude_old_trials.png")

  • Overall, younger participants did better (age, similar: p=0.022; new: p<.001).
  • Adults were marginally more sensitive to the magnitude of negative prediction errors (pe magnitude x age, similar: p=.096; ) but not positive prediction errors (pe sign x pe magnitude x age, similar: p=.002).
  • Children with a positivity bias did marginally better on positive PE trials (pe sign x valence asymm x age, similar: p=.084; pe_sign x valence asymm x age, old: p=.074) ### Let’s now consider lure trials…

How does PE magnitude and sign shape the likelihood that someone will mistake a lure as an old item? or fail to recognize it at all (e.g. answer “new”)?

knitr::include_graphics("memory_plots/valence_asymm_pe_sign_magnitude_lure_trials.png")

  • Items associated with large PEs were less likely to be completely forgotten (pe magnitude, new: p=.0026)
  • Individuals with a positivity bias were less likely to completely forget an item associated with a positive PE (pe sign x valence asymm, new: p=.02)

Do these effects differ with age?

knitr::include_graphics("memory_plots/age_valence_asymm_pe_sign_magnitude_lure_trials.png")

  • Younger participants were less likely to completely forget the target (age, new: p<.001). This was particularly true for items associated with a positive PE (pe sign x age, new: p=.008; similar: p=.093)
  • While older participants as a group did worse than younger participants, those with a positivity bias were more accurate than adults with negativity bias in not confusing a lure with an old item (valence asymm x age, similar: p=.0058)
